name: Marco Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Marco. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead operator on the corrugator at Ashby Packaging. The corrugator is the long machine that glues paper into cardboard sheets, the brown board that boxes are made from. It's a hundred metres long and it runs at about two hundred metres a minute. I set the order changes, keep the steam and glue right, and manage a crew of six. My dad worked thirty years at the paper mill up the road, so I grew up with the smell of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is the crew. We're like a football team, and when a big order goes through clean, we all know it. Hard is the pay. I'm the best on the corrugator and I'm paid less than the Ashby plant in the city. And with the paper mill closed, there's only us left in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it's mostly noise. That's what my dad would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, like a better calculator, and nothing to lose sleep over. At work I'd tell the crew to keep their heads down and do good work. I'm not much for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my worries are the same as now. Rosa (my girlfriend) is a teaching assistant and neither of us earns much. We've got about three weeks saved and the rent went up again. Ashby's had two quiet months this year, and when it's quiet, the overtime goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the corrugator and keep my crew tight, because a good crew keeps a plant open. I'd ask Ashby about the electrical apprenticeship they talk about every year but never start. And I'd use the AI app now and then, like when I checked our tenancy agreement last month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Not worried, just stuck where I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the plant had two quiet months. What did that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred in lost overtime. We skipped Rosa's sister's wedding abroad because of it. She still mentions it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think the apprenticeship never starts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because head office sees it as a cost. My dad did his apprenticeship at sixteen and the mill paid for all of it. Companies used to take the long view.

say: AI is a **useful tool**, like a better calculator, nothing to lose sleep over.
He'd tell the crew to **keep their heads down** and do good work.
think: His worries stay the same: **low pay** for both him and Rosa.
When Ashby is **quiet**, overtime goes first, costing about two hundred.
do: Keep his **crew tight** on the corrugator.
Ask Ashby to start the **electrical apprenticeship**.
Use the **AI app** occasionally for paperwork.
S0.quote: My dad did his apprenticeship at sixteen and the mill paid for all of it. Companies used to take the long view.
fieldNote: He measures today against his father's **paper mill** era.
Two **quiet months** already hurt the household, so AI barely features.
He sees **apprenticeships** as the fair route, not government help.

steps.text: Keep the corrugator crew together and running clean
Ask Ashby to finally start the electrical apprenticeship
Check paperwork like the tenancy agreement with the AI app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office first, then us, slowly. Yeah, that sounds real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, and progress doesn't wait for anyone, so we'd better keep up. At work I'd say the office will feel it before we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the corrugator is closer to the edge than people think. The order changes I do by eye are planned by software already, and an AI would make the line run with four people, not six. So my crew shrinks, maybe not me, but two of my lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Ashby again for the apprenticeship, and if they said no, I'd pay for an evening electrical course myself, about six hundred a year. I'd learn the new planning software as soon as someone showed me it works. And I'd cut back to save a bit, starting with the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for my lads more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the two lads you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny and Kev. Danny's got a baby coming and Kev's only nineteen. I'd fight to keep Danny, and I'd tell Kev to get a trade while he's young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said progress doesn't wait. Do you believe that, or is it what you'd say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I believe it, but I'd want the company to do right by people too. My dad says a company that sacks good men to save a few pounds loses more than it saves.

say: **Progress** doesn't wait, so people had better keep up.
The **office** will feel it before the floor does.
think: AI-planned changes could run the corrugator with **four people**, not six.
His crew would shrink, likely **two of his lads**.
do: Push again for the **apprenticeship**, or pay six hundred for an evening course.
Learn the **planning software** once he sees it works.
feel: **Anxious** for his lads more than himself.
S1.quote: A company that sacks good men to save a few pounds loses more than it saves.
fieldNote: His public line backs **progress**; privately he worries about his crew.
He'd pay for **his own course** if the company won't.
His father's sayings shape his sense of **fairness**.

steps.text: Pay six hundred a year for an evening electrical course
Learn Ashby's new planning software once proven
Sell the car and save the monthly payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Bloody hell. Sorry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have every right to use new machines, but they owe it to their people to train them for what's next. I'd say the government should fund apprenticeships for adults, not just hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2031 a robot can do what my crew does, and the AI already runs the corrugator by 2028. There'd be one man watching screens, and it wouldn't need to be me. I'd be thirty-one, maybe married, with no house and no trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the evening electrical course straight away, even if it means debt. I'd talk to Rosa about moving to the city where there's more work. And I'd ask my dad's old friend who runs an electrical firm whether he'd take me on as an adult apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like when the board starts to wrap and you know the order's ruined.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said debt. How much would you take on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A thousand, maybe. I hate owing money, my dad never did. But a trade is worth a thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rosa say about moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say yes if there's a school that needs her. Teaching assistants are hands-on with kids, so she might be all right longer than me. That's a strange thing to think about.

say: Companies have a **right** to use machines but **owe training** to their people.
Government should fund **adult apprenticeships**, not hand out money.
think: AI runs the corrugator by **2028**, robots do the crew's work by 2031.
He'd be thirty-one with **no house** and no trade.
do: Start the **electrical course** now, even taking on a thousand in debt.
Discuss **moving to the city** with Rosa.
Ask his dad's friend about an **adult apprenticeship**.
feel: **Alarmed**, like watching a board wrap and knowing the order's ruined.
S2.quote: I hate owing money, my dad never did. But a trade is worth a thousand.
fieldNote: He balances **free-market** views with a strong sense of employer duty.
He'd break his rule against **debt** to buy a trade.
Turns to his father's **network** for an apprenticeship.

steps.text: Borrow a thousand to start the evening electrical course
Ask his dad's friend for an adult electrical apprenticeship
Plan a move to the city with Rosa

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to get a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when people find out who's willing to work for their future. I'd tell the young ones at Ashby to get an apprenticeship now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is about right for me. It's enough to finish an electrical qualification by 2030, before the thinking AI comes, and I'd still have three years of hands-on work at Ashby while I get going. I'd want to see one or two others do it first, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the electrical course next autumn, after I've seen how Danny's brother got on with it. I'd put fifty a month aside for tools. And I'd vote for whoever puts money into apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see how Danny's brother got on. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want to spend money on a course that leads nowhere. If he gets a job out of it, I'll follow. If not, I'll look at something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Rosa plan in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting married, probably in the third year, once I've got the trade. My mum would want it in the church where she married my dad.

say: This is when people show who's willing to **work for their future**.
Young workers at Ashby should get an **apprenticeship now**.
think: Five years lets him finish an **electrical qualification** by 2030.
He'd still have **three hands-on years** at Ashby, but wants others to go first.
do: Sign up for the **electrical course** next autumn.
S3.quote: I don't want to spend money on a course that leads nowhere.
fieldNote: Classic **steady** adopter: waits for Danny's brother's result.
He times his **marriage** to Rosa around finishing the trade, in the third year.
Political action is **voting**, focused on apprenticeships.

steps.text: Enrol in the evening electrical course next autumn
Save fifty a month for electrician's tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for every man and woman to learn a new trade, and companies should be part of that. I'd tell the crew we've got time, but not to waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it's fine. I'd get married, get my electrical ticket in a few years, and be wiring robots by the time they come. The only worry is the money in between, because Ashby still pays badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the corrugator job and keep the crew strong. I'd start the electrical course in about two years, once I'd saved a bit. And Rosa and I would marry next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait two years for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because right now I can't afford it without debt, and with ten years I don't need to borrow. Two years of saving fifty a month and the course is paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could change that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Ashby closed early. Plants close for other reasons, cheaper board from abroad or a new owner. Then it's not ten years, it's ten weeks.

say: Ten years is enough for everyone to **learn a new trade**.
He'd tell the crew they have time but **not to waste it**.
think: He'd marry, get an **electrical ticket**, and be wiring robots by 2039.
The worry is **money in between**, with Ashby still paying badly.
do: Keep the **corrugator job** and the crew strong.
Start the **electrical course** in about two years without debt.
S4.quote: Plants close for other reasons, cheaper board from abroad or a new owner.
fieldNote: Long warning lets him avoid **debt**, which matters to him.
He names an **early closure** as the real risk.
Life plans like **marriage** go ahead on time.

steps.text: Keep running the corrugator at Ashby
Save fifty a month for two years to pay for the course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. No time, no money and no trade. What would help is apprenticeships for grown-ups, paid properly, so a man of thirty can learn a trade without his family going short. Not a handout, a ladder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about pride. My dad was proud of the mill. When it shut, he wasn't the same for years. People need work they can be proud of, not just money.

portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old** lead corrugator operator at Ashby Packaging, a cardboard plant.
He lives with Rosa, a **teaching assistant**, on low pay with about three weeks saved.
**Traditional** and steady, he backs free markets but expects employers to train their people.
His father's **closed paper mill** shapes his views on pride, debt and apprenticeships.
He'd move into an **electrical trade**, faster and with debt if warning is short.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: no time, no money and no trade.
whatWouldHelp: Properly paid **adult apprenticeships**, as a ladder rather than a handout.
